# The Korea Invisible Mass Search (KIMS) Experiment: New Constraints on WIMP-Nucleon Interactions

The Korea Invisible Mass Search (KIMS) experiment has established new and competitive limits on the WIMP-nucleon cross section, providing important constraints in the ongoing effort to detect dark matter. These results were derived from a substantial dataset corresponding to a total exposure of 3409 kg·days, representing a significant accumulation of low-background detector operation.

At the heart of the experiment lies an array of low-background CsI(Tl) crystal scintillators, which serve as the primary detection medium for potential dark matter interactions. To minimize interference from cosmic rays and other environmental radiation, the detectors were installed at the Yangyang underground laboratory, where the substantial rock overburden provides effective shielding and a suitably quiet environment for rare-event searches.

Among its key achievements, the KIMS experiment attained the most stringent limit to date on spin-dependent WIMP interactions for the pure proton case. This result underscores the particular sensitivity of the CsI(Tl) target material to spin-dependent couplings involving protons, a channel to which many other dark matter experiments are less responsive.

A further notable outcome of the analysis was the exclusion of the DAMA signal region for WIMP masses above 20 GeV/c². Importantly, this exclusion applies to both spin-independent and spin-dependent interaction scenarios, addressing a long-standing point of contention in the dark matter community regarding the interpretation of the DAMA signal.

Perhaps most significantly, these conclusions were reached by a single experiment employing crystal scintillator technology. Because KIMS uses a detector medium and technique comparable to those of the DAMA experiment, its ability to independently probe and exclude the DAMA-favored parameter space carries particular weight, offering a self-consistent and direct test of the earlier claims.

# The KIMS Search for WIMP Dark Matter with CsI(Tl) Crystal Scintillators

## Introduction

The nature of dark matter remains one of the most compelling open questions in modern physics. Weakly Interacting Massive Particles (WIMPs) represent a leading class of candidates, arising naturally in extensions of the Standard Model such as supersymmetry. Direct detection experiments aim to observe the rare interactions between WIMPs from the galactic halo and target nuclei in terrestrial detectors. The KIMS (Korea Invisible Mass Search) experiment was designed to contribute to this global effort by employing low-background CsI(Tl) crystal scintillators.

## Experimental Setup

The KIMS experiment was conducted at the Yangyang underground laboratory, where substantial rock overburden provides shielding against cosmic-ray-induced backgrounds. The detector array consisted of thallium-doped cesium iodide, CsI(Tl), crystal scintillators, which were carefully selected and processed to achieve exceptionally low levels of internal radioactive contamination. This choice of target material is particularly significant because the presence of both cesium and iodine—nuclei with substantial spin content—makes CsI(Tl) especially sensitive to spin-dependent WIMP interactions, complementing the sensitivity to spin-independent couplings.

For this analysis, the experiment accumulated an exposure of **3409 kg·day** of data. This substantial dataset, combined with the low-background environment and effective discrimination between nuclear recoil signals and electromagnetic backgrounds, enabled a rigorous search for WIMP-induced nuclear recoil events.

## Results and Constraints

By analyzing the collected data and finding no significant excess consistent with a WIMP signal, the KIMS collaboration was able to place stringent upper limits on the WIMP-nucleon interaction cross section. The results are notable in several respects:

- **Spin-dependent interactions (pure proton case):** The experiment established the **most stringent limit** on the spin-dependent WIMP-proton cross section achieved at the time, leveraging the favorable nuclear properties of the cesium and iodine targets.

- **Exclusion of the DAMA signal region:** The DAMA/LIBRA experiment, which also employs sodium iodide crystal scintillators, has long reported an annual modulation signal interpreted as evidence for dark matter. Crucially, the KIMS results **excluded the DAMA-preferred signal region** for both **spin-independent** and **spin-dependent** interactions in the WIMP mass range **above 20 GeV/c²**. This exclusion is especially compelling because it was obtained using the same class of detector technology—crystal scintillators—thereby minimizing systematic uncertainties associated with comparisons across different target materials.

## Significance

The KIMS results represent a significant **single-experiment constraint** on WIMP dark matter using crystal scintillator technology. By probing the DAMA signal region with a comparable detection method, the experiment addressed a central tension in the dark matter field. The combination of a competitive spin-dependent proton limit and the direct exclusion of the DAMA-favored parameter space established KIMS as an important contributor to the worldwide program of dark matter direct detection, demonstrating the power of low-background CsI(Tl) scintillators in the search for physics beyond the Standard Model.

# The Invisible Korea

When people think of Korea, vivid images often come to mind: the neon-lit streets of Seoul, the global phenomenon of K-pop, the sizzling barbecue restaurants, and the sleek technology that has made the nation a symbol of modern innovation. Yet beneath these dazzling surfaces lies another Korea—one that remains largely invisible to the casual observer.

## The Country Behind the Spotlight

The invisible Korea exists in the quiet moments and hidden corners that rarely make it into travel brochures or viral videos. It is the elderly grandmother tending a small vegetable garden in a rural village, far removed from the frenetic energy of the capital. It is the traditional craftsmen who spend decades mastering skills that few outsiders will ever appreciate.

This overlooked Korea also includes the countless workers who power the economy behind the scenes—the delivery riders navigating crowded streets, the factory employees on late-night shifts, and the small business owners keeping neighborhoods alive.

## Invisible Struggles and Silent Strength

The invisible Korea carries stories of resilience. The nation endured colonization, war, and division, experiences that left deep marks on the collective memory. Many older Koreans lived through poverty that younger generations can scarcely imagine, and their sacrifices built the prosperity now taken for granted.

There are also invisible social challenges: loneliness among the elderly, pressures faced by students, and the quiet mental health struggles that many hesitate to discuss openly. These realities exist just beneath the polished image the country projects to the world.

## Seeing the Unseen

To truly understand Korea, one must look beyond the visible spectacle and acknowledge the invisible foundations upon which it stands. The temples hidden in misty mountains, the fading dialects of remote regions, and the unspoken traditions passed quietly between generations all form part of this deeper story.

The invisible Korea reminds us that every nation is more complex than its most famous exports. By seeking out what remains unseen, we gain a richer, more honest appreciation of a country that continues to balance its ancient soul with its modern face.

counterfactuals.output:
# Abstract

We report results from a direct dark matter search conducted by the Korea Invisible Mass Search (KIMS) experiment using an array of low-background CsI(Tl) crystal scintillators located at the Yangyang Underground Laboratory. The detector comprises twelve CsI(Tl) crystals with a total mass of 103.4 kg, operated under an overburden of approximately 2000 meters water equivalent to suppress the cosmic-ray muon flux. Each crystal is read out by two photomultiplier tubes, enabling effective pulse-shape discrimination between nuclear recoil and electron recoil events on the basis of scintillation decay-time characteristics.

With an accumulated exposure of 24,524.3 kg·day, we searched for weakly interacting massive particle (WIMP) induced nuclear recoils in the energy range of 3–11 keV. No significant excess of nuclear-recoil events consistent with a dark matter signal was observed above the expected background. The measured event rate and pulse-shape parameters are consistent with the anticipated backgrounds from radioactive contaminants within the crystals and surrounding materials.

These results are particularly significant for their sensitivity to spin-dependent WIMP interactions on iodine and cesium nuclei. Furthermore, because CsI(Tl) contains the same iodine target as the DAMA/LIBRA experiment, our findings provide a model-independent test of the DAMA annual modulation signal interpreted as WIMP-iodine interactions. Our results exclude the DAMA-preferred parameter region under standard halo assumptions, placing stringent constraints on the WIMP-nucleon cross section and contributing to the resolution of long-standing tensions among direct detection experiments.

# Abstract

We present new results on spin-independent WIMP-nucleon interactions from a direct dark matter search conducted with an array of ultra-low-background NaI(Tl) scintillating crystals operated at a deep underground laboratory under a rock overburden of approximately 1400 m (3600 m water equivalent). Using the same target material as the DAMA/LIBRA experiment, our detector is designed to provide a model-independent test of the long-standing annual modulation signal claimed by that collaboration. The analysis is based on an exposure of 97.3 kg·yr accumulated over three years of stable data-taking, with an average energy threshold of 1.0 keV_ee achieved through improved photomultiplier coupling and pulse-shape discrimination of noise events.

We observe no statistically significant excess of nuclear-recoil-like events above the expected background, which is dominated by ³H, ⁴⁰K, and surface-⁴⁰Pb-²¹⁰ contamination as constrained by a detailed Geant4-based background model. A time-integrated analysis of the low-energy spectrum yields upper limits on the WIMP-nucleon spin-independent elastic scattering cross section, excluding cross sections above 1.4 × 10⁻⁴¹ cm² for a WIMP mass of 10 GeV/c² at 90% confidence level. # Abstract

We report on a search for the annual modulation signal claimed by the DAMA/LIBRA collaboration, using an array of ultra-radiopure NaI(Tl) crystal scintillators with a total target mass of 106 kg. By employing the same target material as DAMA/LIBRA, this experiment provides a model-independent test of their dark matter interpretation, free from the systematic uncertainties associated with comparing different detector media. Over an exposure of 3.2 years, we achieved an energy threshold of 1 keV and a background level of 0.65 counts/day/kg/keV in the region of interest (1–6 keV). A time-dependent likelihood analysis reveals no statistically significant annual modulation consistent with the DAMA/LIBRA signal. Our best-fit modulation amplitude in the 2–6 keV energy interval is (0.0027 ± 0.0037) counts/day/kg/keV, incompatible with the DAMA/LIBRA result of (0.0102 ± 0.0008) counts/day/kg/keV at the 3.3σ level. These findings exclude the standard dark matter interpretation of the DAMA/LIBRA signal under the assumption of a spin-independent, isospin-conserving WIMP–nucleon interaction within the standard galactic halo model. We discuss the implications of these results for the broader landscape of dark matter direct detection and outline prospects for extending sensitivity with continued data-taking.
